subject: Thermodynamics
summary: thermodynamic systems and properties, zeroth law and temperature scales, displacement work along different paths, phase change of water, steam quality from property tables, the T–v diagram, ideal-gas equation, compressibility factor and the van der Waals gas

questions.text: A pressure cooker is on the stove; steam escapes intermittently through the weight valve while the food cooks. Taking the cooker and its contents as the system, it is
solution: Concept: A system is open (a control volume) if mass crosses its boundary; closed if only energy crosses; isolated if neither does.
Heat enters from the stove and steam (mass) leaves through the valve, so mass crosses the boundary: an open system.
Exam tip: A sealed rigid tank being heated is closed; a thermos flask (ideally) is isolated; turbines, nozzles, pumps and compressors are open systems.

questions.text: A thermocouple used as a thermometer gives an emf e = 0.2t − 5 × 10⁻⁴ t² (mV), where t is in °C. It is calibrated to read 0 at the ice point and 100 at the steam point, its scale being linear in e. When the gas thermometer reads 50 °C, the thermocouple thermometer reads (round off to two decimal places) ______
solution: Concept: A thermometer scale linear in its thermometric property: t* = 100 × (e − eice)/(esteam − eice).
Exam tip: Two thermometers agree only at their fixed points; between them they differ when the property is not linear in t. The ideal-gas scale is the reference.

questions.text: Which statement about a quasi-static process is NOT correct?
opts: It is a succession of equilibrium states
It can be shown as a continuous line on a property diagram
Free expansion of a gas into vacuum is a quasi-static process
Work in a quasi-static compression of a gas is ∫p dV
questions.ans: (C) Free expansion of a gas into vacuum is a quasi-static process
solution: Concept: A quasi-static process is carried out infinitely slowly, so the system passes through equilibrium states only.
Free (unresisted) expansion is sudden and far from equilibrium: intermediate states are undefined and cannot be drawn. So (C) is wrong.
Exam tip: ∫p dV gives the work only for a quasi-static process; in free expansion ∫p dV ≠ 0 but the actual work is zero.

questions.text: A gas expands quasi-statically from 0.1 m³ to 0.3 m³ following the law p = c/V², the initial pressure being 600 kPa. The work done by the gas (in kJ) is ______
solution: Concept: W = ∫p dV along the given path.
c = p₁V₁² = 600 × 0.1² = 6 kPa·m⁶
Exam tip: Do not use the polytropic formula blindly; here n = 2, and (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) = (60 − 20)/1 = 40 kJ gives the same result as a check.

questions.text: A gas is held in a vertical cylinder of cross-section 0.01 m² by a frictionless piston of mass 50 kg, as shown; the atmosphere above is at 100 kPa. The gas is heated slowly and its volume increases by 0.002 m³. Take g = 9.81 m/s². The work done by the gas (in J, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: A free piston keeps the gas pressure constant at p = patm + mg/A, so W = pΔV.
Of this, 200 J pushes back the atmosphere and 98.1 J lifts the piston (mgΔh = 50 × 9.81 × 0.2).
Exam tip: Forgetting patm (using only mg/A) is the most common mistake.

questions.text: Wet steam at 1 MPa has a specific enthalpy of 2000 kJ/kg. At 1 MPa, h<sub>f</sub> = 762.8 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2015.3 kJ/kg. Its dryness fraction is about
solution: Concept: For a wet mixture h = hf + x hfg.
Exam tip: 0.992 comes from 2000/2015.3, i.e. forgetting hf. Remember hfg (not hg) multiplies x.

questions.text: Wet steam at 200 kPa has a dryness fraction of 0.85. At 200 kPa, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001061 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.8857 m³/kg. Its specific volume (in m³/kg, round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: v = vf + x(vg − vf) ≈ x vg at low pressure.
Approximation x v<sub>g</sub> = 0.7528, almost the same because v<sub>f</sub> ≪ v<sub>g</sub>.
Exam tip: The approximation fails near the critical point, where vf and vg are comparable.

questions.text: The T–v diagram of water shows the saturation dome with critical point C and one constant-pressure line through the points O, P, Q, R and S. Which statement is correct?
opts: O is compressed liquid, Q is a wet mixture, S is superheated vapour
O is a wet mixture, R is saturated liquid, S is compressed liquid
P is saturated vapour and R is saturated liquid
Q is superheated vapour because its temperature equals that at R
questions.ans: (A) O is compressed liquid, Q is a wet mixture, S is superheated vapour
solution: Concept: Left of the saturated-liquid line: compressed (subcooled) liquid; under the dome: liquid–vapour mixture; right of the saturated-vapour line: superheated vapour.
O lies left of the dome (compressed liquid); P is saturated liquid; Q is a wet mixture; R is saturated vapour; S is superheated.
Along P–Q–R both T and p stay constant (phase change), so the isobar is horizontal inside the dome.
Exam tip: Inside the dome p and T are not independent; you need x (or v, h, s) to fix the state.

questions.text: When ice is heated slowly at a constant pressure BELOW the triple-point pressure, it
opts: melts and the water then freezes again
solution: Concept: On the p–T phase diagram the liquid phase exists only above the triple-point pressure (0.6117 kPa for water).
Below this pressure, the constant-pressure line crosses only the sublimation curve: solid → vapour directly.
Exam tip: Water's fusion line slopes backwards (ice is less dense than water), so raising the pressure lowers the melting point; CO₂ sublimes at 1 atm because its triple point is at 5.1 atm.

questions.text: 0.5 kg of an ideal gas occupies 0.2 m³ at 300 kPa and 87 °C. Taking the universal gas constant as 8.314 kJ/kmol·K, the molar mass of the gas (in kg/kmol, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: pV = mRT gives R; then M = R̄/R.
Exam tip: Using 87 instead of 360 K gives an absurd molar mass of about 6.0; always convert to kelvin.

questions.text: In the van der Waals equation (p + a/v²)(v − b) = RT, the constants a and b account respectively for
opts: the finite volume of the molecules and intermolecular attraction
intermolecular attraction and the finite volume of the molecules
molecular collisions with the wall and molecular vibration
the compressibility of the gas and its specific heat
questions.ans: (B) intermolecular attraction and the finite volume of the molecules
solution: Concept: a/v² is a pressure correction: attraction between molecules reduces the pressure they exert on the wall, so it is added to p.
b is the co-volume: the space taken up by the molecules themselves is subtracted from v.
Exam tip: From the critical-point conditions (∂p/∂v)T = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)T = 0: a = 27R²Tc²/(64pc), b = RTc/(8pc).

questions.text: Nitrogen (R = 0.2968 kJ/kg·K) at 10 MPa and 150 K has a measured specific volume of 0.00375 m³/kg. Its compressibility factor (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Z = pv/(RT) compares the real volume with the ideal-gas volume.
Z < 1: attractive forces dominate at this state (close to the critical point of N₂: 126 K, 3.4 MPa).
Exam tip: With p in kPa, R in kJ/kg·K and v in m³/kg, the units cancel directly.

questions.text: An ideal gas in a sealed rigid container at 200 kPa is heated from 27 °C to 127 °C. Its final pressure is
solution: Concept: Rigid and sealed: m and V constant, so p/T = constant (absolute T).
Exam tip: 940.7 kPa comes from using Celsius temperatures (200 × 127/27). Absolute pressure and absolute temperature, always.

questions.text: A gas expands quasi-statically and polytropically (pV<sup>n</sup> = constant) from 1000 kPa, 0.1 m³ to 200 kPa, 0.4 m³. The work done by the gas (in kJ, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Find n from the end states, then W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1).
n = ln(p₁/p₂)/ln(V₂/V₁) = ln 5/ln 4 = 1.161
Exam tip: The result is very sensitive to n; keep at least three decimals of n (rounding n to 1.16 gives 125.0 kJ).

questions.text: A rigid, insulated tank is divided into two equal parts by a partition. One part contains an ideal gas; the other is evacuated. The partition is removed. For the gas, the work done W and the final temperature T₂ (initial T₁) are
solution: Concept: In free expansion against vacuum there is no resistance, so no work is done; the tank is insulated, so Q = 0.
First law: ΔU = Q − W = 0. For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so T₂ = T₁ (the pressure halves).
Exam tip: p₁V₁ ln 2 is the work of a reversible isothermal expansion between the same states; free expansion is irreversible and does no work.
